claims.text: What the strip looks like Sinus tachycardia is the most common finding; the classic right-heart-strain signs are less common.
claims.quote: Sinus tachycardia is the most common finding

claims.text: Aspects (abnormal in red) Rate: sinus tachycardia — the most common abnormality (44% of patients)
claims.quote: Sinus tachycardia – the most common abnormality (seen in 44% of patients with PE)

claims.text: S1Q3T3: deep S in I, Q and inverted T in III — classic but uncommon
claims.quote: S1Q3T3 pattern (deep S in I, Q and inverted T in III) — classic but uncommon

claims.text: The SI QIII TIII pattern is seen in about 20% and is neither sensitive nor specific for PE
claims.quote: SI QIII TIII pattern – deep S wave in lead I, Q wave in III, inverted T wave in III (20%). This “classic” finding is neither sensitive nor specific for PE

claims.text: Axis: right axis deviation
claims.quote: Right axis deviation, new incomplete RBBB

claims.text: QRS: new incomplete RBBB
claims.quote: Right axis deviation, new incomplete RBBB

claims.text: QRS (LITFL): complete or incomplete RBBB in 18%
claims.quote: Complete or incomplete RBBB (18%)

claims.text: T waves (right heart strain): inversions in V1–V4, ± the inferior leads (II, III, aVF); linked to high pulmonary artery pressures (34%)
claims.quote: Right ventricular strain pattern – T wave inversions in the right precordial leads (V1-4) ± the inferior leads (II, III, aVF). This pattern is associated with high pulmonary artery pressures (34%)

claims.text: Most specific: simultaneous T inversions in the inferior (II, III, aVF) and right precordial (V1–4) leads — specificity up to 99% in one study
claims.quote: Simultaneous T wave inversions in the inferior (II, III, aVF) and right precordial leads (V1-4) is the most specific finding in favour of PE, with reported specificities of up to 99% in one study.

claims.text: P wave: P pulmonale — peaked P in lead II > 2.5 mm (9%)
claims.quote: Right atrial enlargement (P pulmonale) – peaked P wave in lead II > 2.5 mm in height (9%)

claims.text: Rhythm: atrial tachyarrhythmias — AF, flutter, atrial tachycardia (8%)
claims.quote: Atrial tachyarrhythmias – AF, flutter, atrial tachycardia (8%)

claims.text: Normal ECG: around 18% of patients with PE have a completely normal ECG
claims.quote: Around 18% of patients with PE will have a completely normal ECG.

claims.text: The ECG is neither sensitive nor specific enough to diagnose or exclude PE
claims.quote: The ECG is neither sensitive nor specific enough to diagnose or exclude PE

claims.text: Causes (mechanism and diagnoses) What it is: thrombi, typically from the large veins of the legs or pelvis, occluding the pulmonary arteries; risk factors impair venous return, injure the endothelium, or make blood hypercoagulable
claims.quote: Pulmonary embolism (PE) is the occlusion of pulmonary arteries by thrombi that originate elsewhere, typically in the large veins of the legs or pelvis. Risk factors for pulmonary embolism are conditions that impair venous return, conditions that cause endothelial injury or dysfunction, and underlying hypercoagulable states.

claims.text: ECG mechanism: right atrial and ventricular dilation (shifting the heart), RV ischemia, and sympathetic stimulation from pain, anxiety and hypoxia
claims.quote: ECG changes in PE are related to: Dilation of the right atrium and right ventricle with consequent shift in the position of the heart Right ventricular ischaemia Increased stimulation of the sympathetic nervous system due to pain, anxiety and hypoxia

claims.text: Not unique to PE: a similar spectrum of changes may be seen with any cause of acute or chronic cor pulmonale
claims.quote: The ECG changes described above are not unique to PE. A similar spectrum of ECG changes may be seen with any cause of acute or chronic cor pulmonale

claims.text: Symptoms Often acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain (when there is pulmonary infarction)
claims.quote: Emboli often cause Acute dyspnea Pleuritic chest pain (when there is pulmonary infarction)
claims.locator: Symptoms and Signs of Pulmonary Embolism

claims.text: Most common signs: tachycardia and tachypnea
claims.quote: The most common signs of pulmonary embolism are Tachycardia Tachypnea
claims.locator: Symptoms and Signs of Pulmonary Embolism

claims.text: Massive PE may present with hypotension, tachycardia, light-headedness/presyncope, syncope, or cardiac arrest
claims.quote: Massive pulmonary emboli may manifest with hypotension, tachycardia, light-headedness/presyncope, syncope, or cardiac arrest.
claims.locator: Symptoms and Signs of Pulmonary Embolism

claims.text: Many emboli are small, physiologically insignificant, and asymptomatic
claims.quote: Many pulmonary emboli are small, physiologically insignificant, and asymptomatic.
claims.locator: Symptoms and Signs of Pulmonary Embolism

claims.text: Treatment Diagnosis: CT angiography is the preferred imaging test
claims.quote: CT angiography is the preferred imaging technique for diagnosing acute pulmonary embolism.

claims.text: Give anticoagulants when PE is diagnosed or strongly suspected (anticoagulation improves survival)
claims.quote: Because anticoagulation improves survival, patients should be given anticoagulants when PE is diagnosed or strongly suspected.

claims.text: Anticoagulation is the mainstay; thrombolysis or embolectomy for hypotension that does not resolve with fluids, and for selected patients with impaired RV function or escalating oxygen needs
claims.quote: Anticoagulation is the mainstay of therapy for PE. Rapid reduction of clot burden via thrombolytic therapy or embolectomy is indicated for patients with hypotension that does not resolve after fluid resuscitation, and for selected patients with impaired RV function or escalating oxygen requirements.
